  B  
Answer all the questions.  
Answer the following question in about 400-450 words:  
  
2)             Chimamanda Adichie is of the view that, "A man is as likely as a woman to be intelligent,                (10)  
  innovative, creative. We have evolved. But our ideas of gender have not evolved very much". Do  
  you agree with the author's views? Elaborate on your response in the light of the arguments  
  presented within the text.  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO2" / Cognitive Level: "Analysis"  
  
3)             George Orwell contends that the 'sporting spirit' often leads to a false sense of camaraderie,           (10)  
  disguising underlying competitive and nationalistic tensions. Do you think Orwell's observations  
  remain valid in the context of contemporary global sporting events?  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO2" / Cognitive Level: "Analysis"  
  
4)             Read the following passage and write a response to the question asked at the end in 400-450 (10)  
  words (your response should not be a summary but it is required to exhibit critical reflection  
  on the ideas presented in the passage).  
  
  
  When Sriya came home from university after a long semester, she noticed that something had  
  shifted-not in the house itself, but in the spaces between conversations.  
  Her father still read the newspaper at the kitchen table, underlining sentences no one else would  
  ever read. Her mother still reminded her, half-sternly, to eat more fruit. Everything looked the same,  
  yet felt slightly out of sync-like she had stepped into a scene that continued in her absence, but no  
  longer fit her exactly.  
  One evening, her father asked about her plans. Not just job prospects, but life-stability, direction,  
  something firm to hold onto. Sriya hesitated. She spoke about internships, possibilities, maybe  
  taking a gap year, maybe not. Her father nodded politely, but she caught the flicker of confusion in  
  Page 2 of 4

his eyes-why so much uncertainty?  
  That night, she found herself frustrated, though she couldn't say with whom. Was it wrong to still be  
  figuring things out? Her world was built on fluid timelines, evolving roles, and the pressure to stay  
  adaptable. Planning five years ahead felt almost unrealistic. But somewhere beneath her  
  frustration, she also knew her father wasn't trying to control her-he was simply reaching across in  
  the only language he trusted.  
  It took time for Sriya to realize that their exchange wasn't a disagreement, but a difference in how  
  each had learned to navigate the unknown. Her parents grew up believing that hard work and  
  stability were the pillars of a good life. Her generation had been taught to question, to redefine  
  success, to value mental health, creativity, and change.  
  There was no fight between them-just different forms of care.  
  Sriya began to notice the quiet efforts they made: her father forwarding her articles about women in  
  leadership, her mother asking about her friends and their ideas. These were not intrusions; they  
  were invitations. She responded in her own way-explaining how a podcast moved her, helping her  
  father set up a digital wallet, and cooking a meal her mother used to make when she was younger.  
  The distance between them didn't disappear, but it began to breathe.  
  The generation gap, Sriya realized, isn't a wall. It's a shared room with different windows-each  
  offering a view the other may not fully see. But if you sit together long enough, and really listen, the  
  light finds its way in.  
  
  Question:  
  What does Sriya's experience reveal about the generation gap, and how do you think  
  individuals can navigate these differences in a constructive way?  
  
  Course Outcome: "CO4" / Cognitive Level: "Analysis"
